facts.text: On this date in 1867, the U.S. formally took possession of Alaska from Russia. The purchase price was $7.2 million — about 2 cents per acre.
On this date in 1922, the BBC was founded. It now broadcasts in over 40 languages, reaching an estimated 492 million people weekly.
More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka with a 4,000 km radius than outside it — roughly half of humanity clusters in that zone of South and East Asia.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding about 60% of the world's fresh lake water.
Tokyo's greater metropolitan area is home to 37 million people — more than the entire population of Canada, packed into a region smaller than Connecticut.
On this date in 1987, Black Monday's shockwaves hit Asia and Europe — the Dow had already shed 22.6% the day prior, the single largest one-day percentage drop in its history, dwarfing even 1929.

On this date in 1867, the U.S. formally took possession of Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million — about 2 cents per acre. The deal was mocked as 'Seward's Folly' until oil was discovered a century later.
The NYSE's total market cap briefly surpassed the entire U.S. GDP in 1999. It happened again in 2020 — and has stayed that way since.

Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion, the largest in history. Its opening-day market cap of $1.88 trillion made it instantly the world's most valuable public company — larger than Apple, Amazon, and Google combined at the time.
Japan's Nikkei 225 peaked at 38,957 on December 29, 1989. It took 34 years to reclaim that level, finally crossing it again in early 2024.
On this date in 1963, Félicette became the first cat in space — a Parisian stray launched by France, she survived and returned safely, then was euthanized weeks later for brain analysis.
On October 18, 1851, Moby-Dick was published — but the sperm whale it fictionalizes is real: an 80-ton bull rammed and sank the Essex in 1820, then circled back to ram it again.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, but you host around 38 trillion bacterial cells — meaning you are, by count, slightly more microbe than human.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh about 10 million tons on Earth.
Mantis shrimp see with 16 types of photoreceptors — humans have 3 — yet research shows they process color worse than we do, routing the data differently to save brain power.
On this day in 1867, the U.S. took possession of Alaska from Russia — a territory larger than Texas, California, and Montana combined, purchased for less than 2 cents per acre.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the iPhone than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid is simply that old.
On this day in 1922, the BBC was founded. It is older than sliced bread, which wasn't sold commercially until 1928.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Europe's oldest university predates Tenochtitlán by three centuries.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and a full 146 years before the World Wide Web.
Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. Coined by John Koenig in 2012 for *The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows* — proof that naming a feeling is halfway to understanding it.
Apricity (n.): the warmth of sun in winter. A perfectly useful English word from 1623 that somehow fell out of use, leaving us without a name for one of life's small reliefs.
On this day in 1685, Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes — and the word *refugee* entered English almost immediately after, borrowed from French *réfugié*, to describe the Huguenots who fled.
Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word from Tierra del Fuego meaning the look shared by two people who each want the other to initiate something. The language has fewer than a handful of living speakers.

On this day in 1867, the U.S. formally took possession of Alaska — a territory whose name derives from the Aleut *Alyeska*, meaning 'the great land', which is either poetic or an understatement of geological fact.

On this date in 2021, Shiba Inu hit its all-time high after Vitalik Buterin burned 90% of his SHIB airdrop — ~$6.7B worth — by sending it to a dead wallet, making him briefly the largest destroyer of personal wealth in crypto history.
On this date in 2017, Bitcoin's mempool backlog crossed 100,000 unconfirmed transactions as the SegWit activation debate peaked, exposing how a 1MB block limit could paralyze a $100B network.
Bitcoin's UTXO model means you never actually 'send' coins — you destroy old outputs and create new ones. Every wallet balance is a legal fiction layered over a ledger of unspent receipts.

The Ethereum genesis block, mined July 30 2015, contained a hidden message: 'dao fork' — wait, that's block 1920000. The genesis extraData field encoded 'Ethereum' in hex, a quiet signature on a $300B experiment.

Satoshi's known addresses hold ~1.1M BTC that have never moved. Because UTXO timestamps are public, any spend would be detectable within seconds globally — the most watched cold wallet in financial history.
On this date in 2015, Google DeepMind's Atari paper hit Nature — the first time a single neural network matched human performance across 49 different games using only raw pixels as input.
On this date in 2017, the AlphaGo Zero paper published: it reached superhuman Go without any human game data, trained purely through self-play in 40 days.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US households.
The transformer architecture, now the backbone of nearly every frontier AI system, was introduced in 2017 by eight authors at Google. Seven of them have since left to found or lead competing AI labs.
Chinchilla scaling laws (2022) showed most large models were undertrained relative to their size — the field had been building bigger networks when it should have been feeding them more data.
